question: With actual public Node configuration proposals, does the pending-change guard follow ApplyConfChange activation or the internal applied frontier advanced by Node.Advance, when configuration activation is deliberately deferred?
rationale: Compare three explicit caller policies from independently constructed one-voter prefixes: defer ApplyConfChange and withhold Advance; defer ApplyConfChange but call Advance early; and activate first before Advance. A real election and first ProposeConfChange produce the committed entry. All Ready persistence finishes before Advance and no network message is delivered early. Public Node.Status acts as an event-loop barrier after proposal/Advance processing. A second actual configuration proposal reveals whether it is encoded as a configuration entry or replaced by an empty normal entry; record commitment separately. In the early policy, later committed entries are not applied until the first configuration activation completes, and all delivered configuration entries are eventually activated in order. Whether the general Node.Advance overlap permission includes delayed configuration activation remains an explicit semantic question, so observations are conditional and not a finding. New peers are not running and their network traffic is dropped; an uncommitted second proposal in a control is not a liveness failure. Finite Ready deadlines diagnose only driver incompletion.

feedback.answered: The source distinguishes Node early-Advance permission from the stricter wording of RawNode.Advance. The prepared experiment uses Node directly, so no lower-level permission is silently substituted. It also separates internal Applied, actual returned ApplyConfChange calls, encoded second-entry type and commitment; none is inferred from ProposeConfChange returning nil.
remaining: Observe the three policy outcomes in the clean-copy execution, then retain the precise contract applicability gap or formulate a sourced scoped responsibility if justified.
